fatal_flaws: The 17-year multi-outcome panel does not exist. HLS L30 starts April 2013 and S30 starts December 2015. SMAP starts in 2015, ECOSTRESS in mid-2018, and SMAP-HydroBlocks covers only 2015-2019. OpenET reached all 48 states only in December 2025, and how far its CONUS history goes back is unverified. So the headline hindcast cannot work as written: you cannot rank regimes for the 2012 drought from 2008-2011 HLS, Prithvi, SMAP, OpenET or ECOSTRESS data. In 2012 the only Landsat sensor flying was Landsat 7 with its stripe defect (Landsat 5 stopped in late 2011), so winter cover and residue mapping for 2008-2012 is very weak. The example card has the same problem in several places: 'ECOSTRESS ESI below p20 in 4 of the last 10 years' needs 10 years of a sensor that has about 7; the 'field's own 15-year HLS/SMAP/OpenET record' is impossible; and 'pre-2014 satellite trajectory' twins predate HLS.

Defining treatment by future persistence and censoring reversion builds survivorship bias into the design. 'Switch' means 3 or more years of sustained adoption, and reversion is treated as censoring. But farmers drop cover crops mainly because they took a yield hit, which is the outcome being measured, so the censoring is informative. Conditioning on future behaviour selects the fields where the practice worked and pushes estimated effects upward, which is exactly the opposite of the doc's stated aim to 'stop the cover-crop yield penalty'. Callaway-Sant'Anna also assumes adoption is absorbing (once on, always on), and cover-crop adoption is not.

SMAP cannot measure a field-level treatment effect. A 9 km SMAP L4 pixel is about 8,100 ha, roughly 150-200 fields. Every field in a footprint inherits the same value, and with about 4.7% cover-crop adoption the treated share of any footprint is tiny, so a 10% change on one field moves the footprint signal by well under 1%. SMAP L4 root-zone moisture is mostly land-model output (with brightness temperatures assimilated), and the model uses static vegetation and soil parameters that do not know about cover crops. SMAP-HydroBlocks gets its 30 m detail from land model clusters built on soil, topography and land cover, and covers surface moisture in 2015-2019 only. Neither product can encode management, so 'drydown tau +8 to +15%' on twins is an artifact of where fields sit, not an effect of the rotation. The SMAP signpost (April root-zone moisture below p20) also rests on about 11 Aprils of record, so the percentile is unstable.

The three-estimator agreement rule is not independent confirmation and it breaks the stated uncertainty. DiD, generalized synthetic control and causal forest/DML all run on the same proxy outcomes and the same observed covariates, and all depend on no unmeasured confounding or parallel trends, so a shared bias such as operator skill or tile drainage makes them agree on the wrong answer. Showing a number only when all three agree in sign is a selection step. It biases displayed effects away from zero when the true effect is small, and the conformal intervals and badges computed afterwards no longer have their nominal coverage.

The per-field claim outruns the measurement noise. SCYM-style yield proxies explain only a minority of field-level yield variance, while the effects being estimated are 3-5% of yield. Deines et al. needed about 90,000 fields to estimate an average. Synthetic control on one field's noisy annual proxy, or a conformal interval for an individual treatment effect (which needs both potential outcomes), will produce intervals far wider than the card's '-4.5% to +0.3%'. Lei-Candès and Jin-Ren-Candès guarantee marginal coverage, averaged over fields, not per-field conditional coverage, and they assume exchangeability, which spatially and temporally autocorrelated fields violate.

Erosion targets the wrong mechanism. The paper cited for the knoll story, Thaler, Larsen & Yu 2021, attributes A-horizon loss on convex hilltops mainly to tillage erosion, which is not driven by rainfall on bare soil. A dose built from bare-soil fraction x IMERG erosivity (RUSLE-style) mostly misses that process, and a cover crop or rotation change does not stop tillage translocation; reducing tillage would. Strategies 1 and 3 promise to fix the knoll with an exposure metric that does not represent what removed the topsoil.

Reverse causality in the 2019 hindcast. Many 2019 prevented-planting acres were seeded to cover crops under RMA haying and grazing rules, so prevented-planting status causes cover-crop 'adoption'. Using 2019 as a validation year for 'cover crops reduce wet-year losses' scores the model on a loop that runs from outcome to treatment.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Deines et al. 2023 and Kluger et al. 'proved that causal forests on satellite data recover rotation and cover-crop effects'
overclaimed_impacts.problem: Deines' own title says cover crops are 'associated with' yield losses. It is an observational causal forest on 2019-2020 SCYM yields with no cover-crop species or timing data. Kluger 2022 is a hybrid estimator precisely because observational estimates alone were biased: it beat satellite-only estimates by 26% RMSE.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Say these studies 'estimated, under selection-on-observables assumptions', and use Kluger's finding (observational-only estimates do worse) as the motivation for anchoring on trials.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Erosion impact: 35+/-11% of Corn Belt cultivated area has lost its A horizon, worth $2.8+/-0.9B/yr
overclaimed_impacts.problem: This is accumulated damage from historical, mostly tillage, erosion. Rotation or cover-crop choices do not restore lost A horizon, and a bare-soil dose does not track tillage erosion. Putting the $2.8B in the impact table implies the tool can recover some of it.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Present it as context only. Claim impact as avoided future loss in tonnes per hectare per year from a tillage-plus-water erosion model (for example WEPP via the Daily Erosion Project, or a WaTEM/SEDEM tillage term), and add reduced tillage as a regime.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Cover crops and perennials raise infiltration about 59% (Basche & DeLonge 2019)
overclaimed_impacts.problem: In the abstract, 59.2+/-20.9% is the pooled figure for perennials and cover crops. University coverage puts cover crops alone at about 35% (23 studies). The tool mostly recommends cover crops, and SMAP cannot verify either number at field scale.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Quote about 35% for cover crops, keep 59% for perennials, and drop the claim that SMAP 'measures' it.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Farm tier: avoiding half the yield penalty on mistargeted acres is worth 'tens to hundreds of $M/yr' and removes the main reason farmers quit
overclaimed_impacts.problem: The upper bound assumes all 18M cover-crop acres take a $40/ac corn penalty. Many are not in corn that year, $40/ac was a press-release figure, and avoiding the penalty often means dropping the cover crop. That subtracts from the erosion, nitrate, infiltration and insurance benefits claimed in the other tiers. Farm and environmental benefits are counted as if they add up when they partly trade off.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Build a single accounting: decisions changed x CATE difference x realistic uptake, netting yield gains against lost environmental services on acres steered away from covers. Show the trade-off explicitly instead of claiming both sides.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Insurance: a 1 pp rise in county cover-crop adoption is linked to about $40M lower prevented-planting indemnities; PCCP's $5/ac drew 12.2M acres vs a 5M forecast
overclaimed_impacts.problem: Won et al. 2024 is a county-level association for 2005-2016 that peaks in an extreme year, and NC State's release says '1%', not clearly '1 pp'. I could not find the 12.2M-vs-5M figure. Sawadgo 2024 found only 11% of Iowa's discount acres were additional, so large PCCP enrollment mostly signals windfall payments, not success. County associations cannot be packaged as 'field-level actuarial evidence'.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Cite Won as county-level and correlational, check the PCCP numbers against RMA or FSA reports, and use the low additionality to argue for targeting rather than as evidence of uptake.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Diverse rotations: +28% maize yield and 14-90% smaller drought-year losses (Bowles et al. 2020)
overclaimed_impacts.problem: These are maize-phase yields in 11 long-term experiments, often with forage or perennial phases and monoculture baselines. They are not per-rotation-year income, and they do not carry over to oat/clover insertion on commercial corn-soy fields. Kluger et al. 2025, which the doc also cites, finds diversification beyond two crops is typically small or negative.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Show Bowles as trial evidence for the maize phase, next to Kluger 2025's null or negative per-rotation-year effects, and do not attach either to Strategy 2 as a farm benefit.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: SOC trend direction 'correct or stable for about 95% of monitored sites'; SOC shifts from declining to stable on 64% of twins
overclaimed_impacts.problem: Broeg et al. 2024 is German cropland with 100 validation sites. Trend R2 = 0.16, and the 95% depends heavily on the 'stable' class, which is the easy one. Detection time grows as the SOC change gets smaller. A cover-crop change of roughly 0.1-0.3 t C/ha/yr adopted in 2012-2020 is very unlikely to be detectable by about 2025, and the method has not been validated in the U.S.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Drop the per-twin SOC direction claim or label it exploratory, and run a U.S. validation against repeated soil samples (for example, sites with repeated SSURGO or NRCS RaCA-style sampling) before showing it.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Odisha voice advisory RCT shows the delivery channel works (+1.7% yield, 6.8M farmers, $12-19 per $1)
overclaimed_impacts.problem: That RCT tested generic, agronomist-written rice advice, not causal-ML counterfactual rotation advice. The benefit-cost ratio is PxD's own estimate, and the working paper relied partly on vegetation-index yields.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Cite it only as evidence that voice delivery reaches farmers at low cost, not as evidence of the impact of COUNTERFIELD-type content.

overclaimed_impacts.claim: Program targeting gives 'more conservation per EQIP dollar' (WRI auction about 7x phosphorus per dollar)
overclaimed_impacts.problem: The 7x comes from a 2005 Conestoga pilot with 7 auction contracts and 13 EQIP contracts under an artificial budget, with phosphorus modelled by NutrientNet rather than measured. It is the effect of an auction mechanism, not of CATE-based targeting.
overclaimed_impacts.fix: Estimate targeting gains with the tool's own policy-tree value (doubly robust policy evaluation on held-out regions) and cite the auction only as an analogous mechanism.

citation_problems: Thaler, Larsen & Yu 2021 (PNAS) is real, and 35+/-11% and $2.8+/-0.9B check out. But the paper attributes the loss mainly to tillage erosion, which the doc's bare-soil x erosivity mechanism does not capture. The citation undercuts the mechanism it is used to support.
Basche & DeLonge 2019: 59.2% is the pooled perennials-plus-cover-crops response in the abstract. The cover-crop-only figure is about 35% (from university coverage; confirm in the full text).

Deines et al. 2023 is real (GCB 29(3):794-807) and 5.5% maize / 3.5% soy is correct. The '3+ years' condition applies to the maize estimate, and the paper covers 2019-2020 only. The '$40/ac' figure comes from press coverage, as the doc says, but it is then used as if it were a paper result.

Kluger, Owen & Lobell 2022: the 1.02 / 1.18 / 0.84 t/ha and 13% / 26% RMSE figures match secondary summaries of the paper (ERL, doi 10.1088/1748-9326/ac6083). The reference list gives only the arXiv number; add the ERL DOI.

Kluger, Di Tommaso & Lobell 2025: Zenodo gives DOI 10.1088/1748-9326/ae0f45. I could not verify the volume and article number '20:114037'. The doc cites it for a 'median precrop benefit 4.5% across breadbaskets'; I did not verify that number, so check it against the paper.

Broeg et al. 2024 is GCB 30(12):e17608, doi 10.1111/gcb.17608. Cite the DOI instead of the PMC ID. Trend R2 = 0.16 and '95% correct or stable' are accurate, but the paper is German cropland and the doc applies it to U.S. fields.
Won et al. 2024: the '$40M per 1 pp' comes from an NC State press quote that says '1%'. The paper is county-level, 2005-2016, 12 states, and correlational.
PCCP '12.2M acres vs a 5M forecast': RMA program pages confirm $5/ac but I could not find the 12.2M figure or any 5M forecast. Confirm both against RMA or FSA reports, or drop them.
Sawadgo 2024: '11% additional' is right (from a farmer survey), but it supports low additionality of discounts. It does not support the claim that 'targeting matters' in the sense of CATE targeting.

CSB '~16M polygons': this count comes from a third-party GeoParquet version (fiboa, 16.19M after merging polygons), not NASS. CSB fields are 'fully synthetic' and are re-made for each 8-year window (for example 2015-2022 and 2016-2023), so a stable 2008-present field panel requires linking polygons across editions.

Jin, Ren & Candes: the doc reads Gamma as 'switchers about 2.3x more likely to succeed'. In the marginal sensitivity model, Gamma bounds the odds ratio between the propensity to *receive treatment* with and without the hidden factor. It says nothing about the outcome. The paper's 0-value measures evidence against a zero individual effect, not 'reversing a recommendation' across several regimes and outcomes. Also cite the published version (PNAS 2023), not just the arXiv preprint.
Bowles 2020: 28.1% and 14.0-89.9% are correct. The drought range is a reduction in yield loss for maize phases in long-term experiments, not a rotation-level effect.

He, Lu (Lu) & Cowie 2025 (npj Sust. Agric. 3:10): the +36.2% N2O figure for legume covers is correct. The same meta-analysis reports legume covers *raising* yield 16%, which conflicts with the Deines penalty framing. Cite both or explain why the doc prefers one.
Fitzpatrick & Dunn 2019 builds climate analogs for urban areas, not cropland. It is an acceptable methods precedent but not agronomic validation of analog twins.

Missing core precedent: Giannarakis, Sitokonstantinou, Lorilla & Kontoes (NeurIPS-W 2022, arXiv:2211.03179; field-level DML CATE for sustainable practices); Giannarakis et al. CVPR-W 2022 (arXiv:2204.12956; causal ML for crop rotation, which found the rotation effect insignificant); Tsoumas et al. AAAI 2023 (causal evaluation of a deployed agricultural recommendation system).

GEDI L4A is cited to 'anchor cover biomass', but it is a woody and forest above-ground biomass product built from canopy-height waveforms. It cannot resolve low winter cover crops under about 1 m, and its footprints are sparse.
science_errors: SMAP L4 at 9 km and SPL2SMAP_S at 3 km cannot resolve individual fields, and a representativeness-error term does not create field-scale signal. It only widens the error. SMAP L4 root-zone moisture is land-model output, so drydown tau mostly reflects model physics and static parameters. SMAP-HydroBlocks is surface moisture (not root zone), covers 2015-2019 only, and gets its sub-pixel pattern from static land cover, soil and topography, so it is blind to management.

IMERG at 0.1 degrees and 30 minutes smooths peak rainfall intensity, so EI30 (which uses 30-minute maximum intensity at a point) will be systematically low and spatially blurred. That noise feeds straight into the treatment dose, and the measurement error in the dose attenuates the dose-response estimate.

SOC: satellites cannot measure field SOC change directly. Bare-soil reflectance captures surface SOC only on bare days, is confounded by moisture and roughness, and has a long detection time for small changes. The doc labels SOC 'direction only' in some places but then uses per-twin direction shifts (64%) as an effect, which the method cannot support over 2012-2025.

Early rye termination as a signpost-triggered treatment lacks observational support. Termination date detected from HLS in a cloudy April is uncertain by a week or more, and termination timing is not recorded anywhere, so the effect of '14+ days early' cannot be identified from these data.

Selection into cover crops is driven by EQIP or state cost-share, landlord terms, livestock (grazing covers), prior prevented planting, and operator conservation ethic. None of these is well captured by soil, terrain or Prithvi embeddings. 'Operator-cluster fixed effects from contiguous CSB parcels' guesses ownership from field adjacency, and CSB is synthetic and not linked to operators.

PPI requires the gold-labelled sample to be a random draw from the same population as the proxy sample. Yield-monitor uploads (self-selected, tech-adopting farms), RMA unit yields (aggregated across fields and access-restricted) and LTAR or long-term trial plots (not CSB fields) all violate that, so the 'debiased' estimate keeps its bias.

Callaway-Sant'Anna assumes staggered, absorbing adoption, and cover crops switch on and off. Use estimators for non-absorbing treatments (for example de Chaisemartin-D'Haultfoeuille) or an intent-to-treat definition based on first adoption.

Spillovers: neighbour continuous-corn share as a rootworm exposure map is reasonable, but rotation itself changes neighbours' exposure. The 2012 and 2019 events are landscape-wide shocks that correlate outcomes across all units, so treating fields as independent overstates the effective sample size.

Climate transport: integrating today's CATE over 2045 effect modifiers assumes the effects stay the same given those modifiers, with no change in cultivars, planting dates, CO2 response or management. Analog twins in Kansas or Missouri with 'same soil/terrain' as central Iowa Mollisols will be few, and they differ in irrigation, drainage and operations.

Small-grain insertion in central Iowa covers well under 1-2% of cropland, so calling it one of 3 regimes 'that have real support' is doubtful at a 6-10 county scale. Overlap will be thin and the synthetic-control donor pool tiny.

Strategy 3 (prairie strips) is labelled 'beyond the evidence', but randomized watershed experiments exist (Iowa State STRIPS, Schulte et al. 2017 PNAS). The pipeline ignores RCT evidence that does not come from satellite twins, which contradicts the claim that it uses the best available evidence.

The red-clover card claims 'lower N2O than adding more legume cover with full N'. He et al. 2025 report +36% N2O for legume covers, and a sidecar 'calibrated so that its predicted yield and water effects match L3' says nothing about its N2O accuracy.
novelty_threats: Kluger, Owen & Lobell 2022 and Kluger, Di Tommaso & Lobell 2025: field-level causal ML for precrop effects with satellite yields, a trial-satellite hybrid, and climate heterogeneity. The doc names them, but they cover most of the 'causal core plus heterogeneity by weather' claim already.
Deines et al. 2023: causal forest heterogeneity of cover-crop effects on 90k U.S. fields, with soil and weather drivers. This is the 'per-field CATE shows where covers cost yield' claim.

Giannarakis, Sitokonstantinou et al. 2022 ('Personalizing Sustainable Agriculture with Causal ML', NeurIPS CCAI best proposal; CVPR-W 2022 crop rotation causal ML) and Tsoumas et al. AAAI 2023: field-level CATE recommendations and causal evaluation of a deployed agricultural recommender. Not cited.

Regrow (OpTIS + DNDC), Indigo (DayCent), CIBO (SALUS), Truterra, Agoro: satellite practice detection plus outcome modelling and baselines. The doc notes these are process-model counterfactuals, but buyers will see them as the same product category.

Iowa State Daily Erosion Project: WEPP with radar rainfall, LiDAR and satellite residue and tillage by rotation, at HUC-12 scale across the Midwest. It already does erosion with measured residue cover, and models water erosion better than a RUSLE-style dose.

Agricultural Conservation Planning Framework (ACPF, USDA ARS) and Profit Zone Manager / AgSolver-style precision conservation: field-scale siting of prairie strips and buffers and of low-profit acres to convert. This is Strategy 3 and the landscape targeting layer.

Data-Intensive Farm Management (DIFM) and Practical Farmers of Iowa cooperator strip trials: on-farm randomized trial networks that already produce field-specific causal evidence for management. This is the 'VOI then strip trial' loop.
NASA Acres and NASA Harvest: the operational satellite layers (cover crop, tillage, SOC) the doc consumes. Their teams overlap heavily with the Lobell lineage and could add decision support.
NRCS Conservation Assessment Ranking Tool (CART) and EQIP ranking: existing targeting machinery that any policy-tree output would have to plug into or replace.
strongest_upgrades: Rebuild the timeline around data that exists. Make the causal panel 2016-2025 (HLS L30+S30, OpenET where its history holds, SMAP only as a regional moisture modifier), with Landsat-only SCYM and CDL for 2008-2015 restricted to the crop-sequence regimes. Replace the 2012 hindcast with an out-of-time test on the 2023 central-Iowa flash drought or the 2021-22 western Corn Belt drought, trained on 2016-2020. Remove every card statement that implies more years of record than a sensor has.

Fix the treatment definition. Use intent-to-treat at first adoption. Model disadoption as a competing outcome and correct with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights. Use estimators for non-absorbing staggered treatments (de Chaisemartin-D'Haultfoeuille / did_multiplegt) instead of conditioning on 3+ years of persistence.

Add identification that does not depend on selection-on-observables. Program rollouts and funding shocks give near-random variation in adoption: Iowa's discount program start (2017), PCCP 2021, EQIP ranking-score cutoffs (regression discontinuity), and county or state cost-share budget exhaustion. Use them for IV, encouragement or RD designs. This changes the method from 'three estimators agree' to 'an observational estimate checked against a quasi-experiment', which reviewers will take seriously.

Replace the agreement rule with a pre-registered primary estimator plus a calibrated badge. Run a semi-synthetic benchmark, with spatially structured hidden confounders, to learn how often each diagnostic pattern (estimator disagreement, Gamma, overlap) goes with real error. Then map badges to measured error rates and report coverage after selection.

Report at the level the data supports. Give group effects by field type (soil x landscape position x weather regime) with honest intervals, and make the per-field output a statement that the field belongs to a type, plus trial-based updating. Drop individual-effect intervals for single fields unless farmer yield-monitor data exist.

Bring randomized evidence in as a first-class input: Practical Farmers of Iowa cover-crop strip trials (since 2009), DIFM on-farm trials, LTAR and long-term rotation experiments, and STRIPS for prairie strips. Use Kluger's hybrid as the core estimator, not an add-on, so Strategy 3 is no longer 'beyond the evidence'.

Fix the erosion science. Replace the bare-dose x RUSLE exposure with a tillage-plus-water erosion model (Daily Erosion Project WEPP outputs, plus a tillage translocation term driven by curvature and NDTI-detected tillage intensity). Add reduced or no-till as a regime, since it addresses the knoll mechanism Thaler identified.

Drop the SMAP-derived field outcomes (drydown tau, storm gain) and keep SMAP and GRACE as regional modifiers and signposts. If infiltration matters, use ECOSTRESS/OpenET ET partitioning or Sentinel-1 SAR at 10-20 m as a field-scale moisture proxy, and validate against SCAN or in-situ probes.

Rebuild the impact table as tool-attributable impact with no double counting: decisions changed x difference in effects x uptake, with farm yield and environmental services netted against each other on acres steered away from covers. Label meta-analysis practice effects as 'practice effect', not 'tool impact'. Verify or drop the PCCP 12.2M/5M figures, and correct Basche (35% for cover crops) and Gamma's meaning.

Position against the closest prior work explicitly (Giannarakis/Sitokonstantinou/Tsoumas, Lobell lab, Daily Erosion Project, ACPF, DIFM). Name the genuinely new pieces as the claimed contribution: quasi-experimental program instruments, trial-hybrid group effects, decision-theoretic VOI that routes farmers to strip trials, and signpost monitoring.
